newsitem.title: BELGIUM: France and Germany push EU on foreign policy.
newsitem.headline: France and Germany push EU on foreign policy.

text.p: Three months before European Union treaty talks are due to end, negotiators appear finally to be making progress in the area of foreign policy.

France and Germany, always keen to be on the same page in EU affairs, presented plans on Monday calling for creation of a more public face for the EU's diplomacy and for advance preparations in dealing with crises abroad.
They also called for the gradual incorporation of the Western European Union (WEU) defence grouping into the EU proper.

Although a number of countries -- notably sovereignty conscious Britain and neutrals like Sweden -- are wary of further integration in the military and foreign policy fields, others are coming closer together.
"The elements of an agreement are clearly taking shape," Dutch European Affairs Minister Michiel Patijn said on Tuesday after the main treaty-negotiating committee had discussed the proposals.
Patijn chairs the committee, which is due to present a new treaty to EU leaders at a summit in June in Amsterdam.

Under the plan proposed by Paris and Bonn and supported by Spain, Italy and Belgium among others, the EU would draw up a list of "common strategies" in certain areas without waiting for a crisis to erupt or take the bloc by surprise.
The list would be limited, French European Affairs Minister Michel Barnier said, in order to ensure that common foreign policy fell strictly in areas of interest to the whole Union.

EU enlargement, relations with Russia, the Balkans and the Mediterranean basin would be included, he said. But areas such as the Middle East and Africa, where there are no lack of disputes, may be left out.
Responsibility for coordinating EU policy would fall to a senior high-profile official, an idea pushed by France and, despite earlier reservations, now more or less endorsed by Germany.
Foreign policy decisions, strategic goals and the methods for achieving them would be agreed unanimously among EU states.
But once a list of policies had been agreed, they would be implemented by majority vote in order to avoid the EU's well-documented penchant for paralysis.
As well as focusing on foreign policy, France and Germany also proposed the progressive inclusion of the WEU into the main bloc.
They did not suggest an eventual deadline for the incorporation to take place, but Werber Hoyer, Germany's negotiator, said it could be within 10 years.

WEU membership would be limited to those EU countries that are also members of NATO, in order to avoid having neutrals -- Austria, Sweden, Finland and Ireland -- weakening the military group's security guarantees.
Agreement, officials said, was by no means unanimous among the 15 EU members in part because Britain remained firmly opposed to an extension of majority voting or the integration of the WEU.
But, they said, the contours of an agreement were there.
